screens.title: Why version control matters for C projects
screens.narratorSegment: Version control is a foundational tool for software development because it transforms an unordered set of files into an auditable history you can navigate. For C projects this matters even more: compiled artifacts, header dependencies, and platform-specific builds create many moving parts. Git records commits, which are snapshots of your project state, so you can return to a known working version when a bug appears. A practical example: imagine you added a new utility function that breaks compilation. With Git, you can inspect recent commits to find the change, revert only the problematic commit, or branch to continue developing without blocking the mainline. A common misconception is that version control is only for teams. In truth, even solo developers benefit from the safety and traceability commits provide. Another misconception is to treat commits like backups; while they serve as checkpoints, good commit hygiene and remote backups matter too. Key practices to adopt are frequent, focused commits, descriptive messages, and using. gitignore to avoid storing build artifacts or secrets. Consider this: when you’re debugging, would you rather sift through filesystem copies or read a clear sequence of commits with purposeful messages? That clarity makes maintenance and collaboration far easier.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.3 › Why version control matters
Core Concept

Why version control matters for C projects

Version control provides history, accountability, and a safe workspace for experiments and collaboration.

Concrete benefits
  • Recover a working compile state after a regression.
  • Work on new features in branches without disrupting main code.
  • Share and synchronize code with teammates through remotes.
Analogy
Commits are like saved checkpoints in a game — you can return to them if something breaks.
Common Mistake
Relying on occasional full-directory copies instead of proper commits makes history hard to read and merge.
Scenario
You add a new header and function, compilation fails. Use git log to find the commit, isolate the change, and either revert it or fix it on a branch.
Key Takeaway

Git reduces risk: it gives you the power to experiment and to restore a stable state when needed.

screens.title: The three Git states
screens.narratorSegment: A fundamental mental model when using Git is the three-area workflow: the working directory, the staging area, and the local repository. The working directory is where you edit files. Those edits are only local changes until you stage them. Staging — using git add — selects which changes will be recorded in the next commit. Think of staging as preparing a curated patch: you decide what belongs in the next snapshot. The local repository is where commits are stored; once you run git commit the staged snapshot becomes a permanent entry in your project history. A concrete example: you modify main. c and utils. c but only want to commit the bugfix in main. c. You run git add main. c and then git commit with a message describing the fix. A common misconception is that git add immediately records history; it does not. Another misconception is that all modified files must be committed at once — staging gives you fine-grained control. Finally, always run git status to verify which files are modified, staged, or untracked before committing. This model will guide safe and precise commits.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.3 › The three Git states
Definition

Working, Staging, Local

Working Directory
Your current files and unsaved edits.
Staging Area
Select changes to include in the next commit using git add.
Local Repository
Where commits are stored permanently after git commit.
Example
You change two files but only stage one. Use git add file to stage the intended change, then git commit with a message describing just that change. This keeps commits focused and reviewable.
Misconception

git add does not create a commit. It only marks changes for the next commit. Use git status to confirm staging.

Check Your Understanding
What command shows which files are staged or modified? (Hint: try it before committing.)

screens.title: Initializing a repository and starting tracking
screens.narratorSegment: To begin tracking a C project you initialize a Git repository in the project directory using git init. This command creates the hidden. git directory that stores all of Git’s metadata and commit objects. A concrete example: create a folder my_c_git_project, change into it, and run git init. Next, create your initial files like main. c and a. gitignore to exclude compiled objects and executables. Use git add to stage the files and git commit with a clear message to create the first snapshot. A good initial commit message might be 'Initial commit: Add main. c and. gitignore'. A common beginner mistake is forgetting to add. gitignore before committing, which can lead to compiled binaries being recorded. If that happens, you should remove the file from history rather than leaving binaries tracked. After the first commit, use git status and git log to confirm the repository state. These first steps set the pattern for disciplined, traceable development. Initializing a repository and starting tracking means git init creates the .git metadata store; stage files and commit to record the first project snapshot.. In practical terms, git init, .git directory, and first commit. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.3 › Initializing a repository
Process Flow

Init → Add → Commit

1. Create project folder and run git init to create .git.
2. Create code files and a .gitignore for object files and executables.
3. Stage files with git add and commit with git commit -m 'message'.
Example Commands
mkdir my_c_git_project && cd my_c_git_project
 git init
 echo "*.o" > .gitignore
 echo "a.out" >> .gitignore
 git add main.c .gitignore
 git commit -m "Initial commit: Add main.c and .gitignore"
Key Takeaway

Initialize early, create .gitignore before adding, and commit a clean initial snapshot.

screens.title: Staging and committing C files
screens.narratorSegment: Staging and committing are the everyday actions you will perform most often. Use git add to move specific edits from the working directory into the staging area; use git commit to record those staged edits into the local repository. Commit messages should explain what changed and why — short, descriptive, and readable by collaborators or your future self. A bad message like 'updates' is useless; a better message is 'Implement input validation in main. c' because it describes both the change and intent. A concrete walkthrough: after editing main. c to add input checks, run git status to confirm modified files, then git add main. c to stage only that change, and git commit -m 'fix: add input validation to main' to snapshot it. If you staged several files by mistake, git restore --staged file will unstage them. A common misconception is that larger commits are always better; instead, prefer small, logical commits so each snapshot is reviewable and easier to bisect when debugging. Consistent commit hygiene accelerates collaboration and reduces cognitive load. Staging and committing C files means stage intentionally and commit frequently with clear messages so history is readable and problems are easier to find.. In practical terms, git add, git commit, and writing useful commit messages. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Module 6 › Chapter 6.3 › Staging and committing C files
Code Walkthrough

Stage → Commit with purpose

# after editing main.c
 git status
 git add main.c
 git commit -m "fix: add input validation to main"
Use git status to confirm what is staged. If you accidentally staged a file, run git restore --staged <file> to unstage.
Commit message tips
  • Start with a short summary that explains the change.
  • Keep messages focused on single logical changes.
  • Prefer present tense and include intent when helpful.
Common Mistake

Large, unfocused commits make it hard to identify which change introduced a bug.

screens.title: Viewing commit history with git log
screens.narratorSegment: Reading your project's history is essential for debugging and understanding how the code evolved. The command git log shows the full history with commit hashes, authors, dates, and messages. For a compact visual of branches and merges, use git log --oneline --graph --decorate. This displays each commit on a single line with an ASCII graph that indicates branch structure and where you are in the commit graph. A concrete example: after making a few commits on a feature branch and merging, you can run git log --oneline --graph --decorate to see how commits from the feature and main lines relate. A common misconception is that only verbose logs are useful; concise oneline graphs often give the best quick overview, while full logs are better when you need detailed timestamps or diffs. You can inspect a single commit with git show to see file changes included in that snapshot. Regularly scanning the log keeps you aware of repository shape and helps prepare meaningful pull requests or code reviews. In practical terms, use log views to audit history and track changes. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Module 6 › Chapter 6.3 › Viewing commit history
Process Flow

git log basics

git log
 git log --oneline --graph --decorate
 git show <commit-hash>
Use the compact graph form for branch overviews and git show when you need the diff for a particular commit.
Example
After merging a feature branch, run git log --oneline --graph --decorate to verify the merge commit and confirm both lines are present.
Pro Tip

Use aliases or a GUI for complex history views, but learn the oneline graph for quick mental maps of your repo.

screens.title: Undoing changes safely
screens.narratorSegment: Undoing mistakes is an everyday need, and Git provides several targeted commands. If you modified a file but haven’t staged it and want to revert, use git restore filename to discard working-directory changes and return the file to the last committed state. If you staged changes but haven’t committed, git restore --staged filename moves them back to the working directory. When you already committed and need to change history, git reset can move the HEAD pointer. git reset --soft HEAD~1 will undo the last commit but keep the changes staged; this is useful to correct your last commit message or group commits differently. git reset --hard HEAD~1 will move the pointer and discard changes in the working directory — this is destructive and cannot be recovered through normal Git operations. A common misconception is that reset always alters the remote. It only rewrites local history; pushing a rewound branch requires care. Always verify with git status and consider creating a branch before destructive operations. These tools let you recover from common errors when used carefully. Undoing changes safely means use restore for discarding edits, reset for moving head; prefer non-destructive options and avoid reset --hard unless certain.. In practical terms, git restore, git reset, and the dangers of --hard. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.3 › Undoing changes safely
Commands
# Discard unstaged edits
 git restore filename

# Unstage staged changes
 git restore --staged filename

# Undo last commit but keep changes staged
 git reset --soft HEAD~1

# Undo last commit and discard changes (destructive)
 git reset --hard HEAD~1
Always check git status before and after these commands to avoid accidental data loss.
Safety Note
git reset --hard permanently discards uncommitted work from your working directory. Use it only when you are certain you do not need those edits.
Common Mistake

Using destructive resets when a simple restore or soft reset would suffice leads to lost work.

screens.title: Branching: isolate features and parallel work
screens.narratorSegment: Branching is the mechanism Git uses to create separate lines of development so you can work on a feature or fix without affecting the main code. A branch is simply a movable pointer to a commit. The typical workflow is to create a branch for a feature, make commits there, and merge back when ready. For example, run git branch feature/add-greeting to create the branch and git checkout feature/add-greeting to switch to it, or use git checkout -b to create and switch in one step. Work there by making commits; the main branch remains stable. A common misconception is that branches are expensive or slow; in Git they are inexpensive and encouraged. Another subtle point: always base your branch on the correct branch (usually main) to minimize surprises. Keeping branches focused on a single task makes reviews and merges easier. Consider branching for experimental changes, refactors, or bug fixes so you can test and iterate without interrupting others. Branching: isolate features and parallel work means create lightweight branches to isolate features, enabling parallel work and safer integration back into main.. In practical terms, create and switch branches to develop independently. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

screens.title: Merging and resolving conflicts
screens.narratorSegment: Merging brings changes from one branch into another. The basic flow is to switch to the target branch, usually main, and run git merge feature-branch. Git will attempt to combine changes automatically. If the same lines in a file were changed differently on both branches, a merge conflict occurs and Git will pause for manual resolution. Conflicts require you to open the affected files, inspect the differing sections, and decide the correct combined content, then mark the file as resolved with git add and complete the merge with git commit. A concrete scenario: you and a colleague both modified main. c in different branches, changing the same function header. During merge, Git flags conflicts; you open main. c, pick the correct logic or combine both improvements, stage, and commit. A common misconception is that merge conflicts are errors; they are normal and an opportunity to decide intended behavior. When merges are frequent and complex, prefer smaller, focused branches and more frequent merges or rebases to reduce conflict surface. Always run tests or compile after resolving conflicts to verify correctness. Merging and resolving conflicts means merging integrates branch work; conflicts are normal and require deliberate resolution and testing to ensure correctness.. In practical terms, combine completed work and handle conflicting edits. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. screens.title: Remote repositories: push and pull
screens.narratorSegment: Remote repositories let you share commits with collaborators and keep safe backups. After creating a remote repository on a hosting platform, you connect it to your local project using git remote add origin remote_repository_URL. To upload your commits, use git push -u origin main where the -u flag sets the upstream branch so future pushes can use git push without specifying origin. To bring changes from the remote into your local branch use git pull origin main. Pull is a convenience that fetches changes and then merges them into your current branch. A concrete use case: when a teammate pushes a hotfix to main, you git pull to bring that fix into your local copy before you continue feature work. A common misconception is that push overwrites others automatically — push will be rejected if your local history is behind; in that case you must git pull and resolve differences before pushing. For safety, avoid force-pushing unless you understand history rewriting and its consequences for collaborators. screens.title: .gitignore and protecting sensitive data
screens.narratorSegment: A. gitignore file tells Git which files or patterns to ignore so they are not tracked. For C projects you typically ignore compiled object files, executables, and temporary build artifacts. Example entries are '*. o' to ignore object files and 'a. out' or your binary name to ignore compiled executables. Beyond build artifacts,. gitignore is critical for preventing accidental commits of sensitive configuration or A P I keys. If you accidentally stage a file with secrets, use git restore --staged to remove it from staging and git restore to revert your working copy to the last committed state. A key safety rule is: never commit secrets to a public repository. If a secret was committed previously, removing it from history is more complex and requires rewriting history and careful coordination with collaborators. Therefore, put. gitignore in place early, and verify with git status that sensitive files are not tracked. Habitually checking status before committing reduces the chance of accidental exposure. .gitignore and protecting sensitive data means use .gitignore to exclude compiled artifacts and secrets; verify with git status and avoid committing sensitive data.. In practical terms, keep compiled objects and secrets out of version control. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. Activity: Initialize and merge

Follow these commands in sequence to practice the workflow with the provided C files.

fullNarratorScript:
In this lesson we learn why Git is essential for C development and how it lets you track changes, collaborate with teammates, and recover from mistakes. Git records commits as snapshots, so you can iterate on code, test features on branches, and merge when ready. You will see concrete commands that initialize a repository, stage files for the next commit, record snapshots with clear messages, inspect the commit history, undo uncommitted or committed changes, and use branching to isolate work. We’ll also cover pushing to and pulling from remote repositories so you can back up work and share it with others. For practice, there is a short hands-on walkthrough using a small C program and utility files, plus a safety checklist showing how to avoid committing secrets and how. gitignore prevents binary clutter. By the end of this chapter you’ll understand the three core Git areas — working directory, staging area, and local repository — and be able to perform the basic workflow reliably. Think of Git as a mental model and toolset: one that turns file changes into a safe, auditable history. How will you use commits and branches to make your next C project safer?

By the end of this chapter you will be able to initialize a Git repository for a C project, stage changes, commit meaningful snapshots, and inspect the history of those commits. You’ll also learn how to undo mistakes safely using restore and reset commands and when each is appropriate. Branching and merging will let you isolate new features and combine completed work back into your main line, and you’ll practice the basic push and pull workflow to sync with remote repositories for collaboration and backup. Each objective ties to a practical skill: initializing a repo gets your project under version control; staging and committing encapsulate changes into traceable units; reading git log helps you audit progress; undo commands let you recover from errors. You will see short examples for each command and a mnemonic to help remember the three Git areas. Finally, there is an emphasis on safe practices like clear commit messages and using. gitignore to protect sensitive data. These skills make development safer and more collaborative.

This second objectives screen focuses on concrete practices and safety: using git status to confirm staged files, writing descriptive commit messages, and maintaining a clean working tree with. gitignore. You’ll practice the common workflow: edit files, run git status to examine what changed, stage the intended files with git add, and commit with a message that explains what and why. We’ll also cover how to undo work carefully: git restore for discarding unstaged edits, git restore --staged to unstage, and git reset when you need to move the HEAD pointer. You will learn the consequences of git reset --hard and why it is destructive. Another important objective is learning to push and pull to a remote repository and configure an upstream branch. Finally, we’ll reinforce good habits: commit small logical changes, avoid committing secrets, and use. gitignore to keep binaries and keys out of version control. These practical habits prevent data loss and make teamwork more efficient.

Version control is a foundational tool for software development because it transforms an unordered set of files into an auditable history you can navigate. For C projects this matters even more: compiled artifacts, header dependencies, and platform-specific builds create many moving parts. Git records commits, which are snapshots of your project state, so you can return to a known working version when a bug appears. A practical example: imagine you added a new utility function that breaks compilation. With Git, you can inspect recent commits to find the change, revert only the problematic commit, or branch to continue developing without blocking the mainline. A common misconception is that version control is only for teams. In truth, even solo developers benefit from the safety and traceability commits provide. Another misconception is to treat commits like backups; while they serve as checkpoints, good commit hygiene and remote backups matter too. Key practices to adopt are frequent, focused commits, descriptive messages, and using. gitignore to avoid storing build artifacts or secrets. Consider this: when you’re debugging, would you rather sift through filesystem copies or read a clear sequence of commits with purposeful messages? That clarity makes maintenance and collaboration far easier.

A fundamental mental model when using Git is the three-area workflow: the working directory, the staging area, and the local repository. The working directory is where you edit files. Those edits are only local changes until you stage them. Staging — using git add — selects which changes will be recorded in the next commit. Think of staging as preparing a curated patch: you decide what belongs in the next snapshot. The local repository is where commits are stored; once you run git commit the staged snapshot becomes a permanent entry in your project history. A concrete example: you modify main. c and utils. c but only want to commit the bugfix in main. c. You run git add main. c and then git commit with a message describing the fix. A common misconception is that git add immediately records history; it does not. Another misconception is that all modified files must be committed at once — staging gives you fine-grained control. Finally, always run git status to verify which files are modified, staged, or untracked before committing. This model will guide safe and precise commits.

To begin tracking a C project you initialize a Git repository in the project directory using git init. This command creates the hidden. git directory that stores all of Git’s metadata and commit objects. A concrete example: create a folder my_c_git_project, change into it, and run git init. Next, create your initial files like main. c and a. gitignore to exclude compiled objects and executables. Use git add to stage the files and git commit with a clear message to create the first snapshot. A good initial commit message might be 'Initial commit: Add main. c and. gitignore'. A common beginner mistake is forgetting to add. gitignore before committing, which can lead to compiled binaries being recorded. If that happens, you should remove the file from history rather than leaving binaries tracked. After the first commit, use git status and git log to confirm the repository state. These first steps set the pattern for disciplined, traceable development. Initializing a repository and starting tracking means git init creates the .git metadata store; stage files and commit to record the first project snapshot.. In practical terms, git init, .git directory, and first commit. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Staging and committing are the everyday actions you will perform most often. Use git add to move specific edits from the working directory into the staging area; use git commit to record those staged edits into the local repository. Commit messages should explain what changed and why — short, descriptive, and readable by collaborators or your future self. A bad message like 'updates' is useless; a better message is 'Implement input validation in main. c' because it describes both the change and intent. A concrete walkthrough: after editing main. c to add input checks, run git status to confirm modified files, then git add main. c to stage only that change, and git commit -m 'fix: add input validation to main' to snapshot it. If you staged several files by mistake, git restore --staged file will unstage them. A common misconception is that larger commits are always better; instead, prefer small, logical commits so each snapshot is reviewable and easier to bisect when debugging. Consistent commit hygiene accelerates collaboration and reduces cognitive load. Staging and committing C files means stage intentionally and commit frequently with clear messages so history is readable and problems are easier to find.. In practical terms, git add, git commit, and writing useful commit messages. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Reading your project's history is essential for debugging and understanding how the code evolved. The command git log shows the full history with commit hashes, authors, dates, and messages. For a compact visual of branches and merges, use git log --oneline --graph --decorate. This displays each commit on a single line with an ASCII graph that indicates branch structure and where you are in the commit graph. A concrete example: after making a few commits on a feature branch and merging, you can run git log --oneline --graph --decorate to see how commits from the feature and main lines relate. A common misconception is that only verbose logs are useful; concise oneline graphs often give the best quick overview, while full logs are better when you need detailed timestamps or diffs. You can inspect a single commit with git show to see file changes included in that snapshot. Regularly scanning the log keeps you aware of repository shape and helps prepare meaningful pull requests or code reviews. Viewing commit history with git log means use git log and compact graph views to understand commit sequences, branches, and merge points for debugging and review.. In practical terms, use log views to audit history and track changes. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Undoing mistakes is an everyday need, and Git provides several targeted commands. If you modified a file but haven’t staged it and want to revert, use git restore filename to discard working-directory changes and return the file to the last committed state. If you staged changes but haven’t committed, git restore --staged filename moves them back to the working directory. When you already committed and need to change history, git reset can move the HEAD pointer. git reset --soft HEAD~1 will undo the last commit but keep the changes staged; this is useful to correct your last commit message or group commits differently. git reset --hard HEAD~1 will move the pointer and discard changes in the working directory — this is destructive and cannot be recovered through normal Git operations. A common misconception is that reset always alters the remote. It only rewrites local history; pushing a rewound branch requires care. Always verify with git status and consider creating a branch before destructive operations. These tools let you recover from common errors when used carefully. Undoing changes safely means use restore for discarding edits, reset for moving head; prefer non-destructive options and avoid reset --hard unless certain.. In practical terms, git restore, git reset, and the dangers of --hard. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Branching is the mechanism Git uses to create separate lines of development so you can work on a feature or fix without affecting the main code. A branch is simply a movable pointer to a commit. The typical workflow is to create a branch for a feature, make commits there, and merge back when ready. For example, run git branch feature/add-greeting to create the branch and git checkout feature/add-greeting to switch to it, or use git checkout -b to create and switch in one step. Work there by making commits; the main branch remains stable. A common misconception is that branches are expensive or slow; in Git they are inexpensive and encouraged. Another subtle point: always base your branch on the correct branch (usually main) to minimize surprises. Keeping branches focused on a single task makes reviews and merges easier. Consider branching for experimental changes, refactors, or bug fixes so you can test and iterate without interrupting others. Branching: isolate features and parallel work means create lightweight branches to isolate features, enabling parallel work and safer integration back into main.. In practical terms, create and switch branches to develop independently. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Merging brings changes from one branch into another. The basic flow is to switch to the target branch, usually main, and run git merge feature-branch. Git will attempt to combine changes automatically. If the same lines in a file were changed differently on both branches, a merge conflict occurs and Git will pause for manual resolution. Conflicts require you to open the affected files, inspect the differing sections, and decide the correct combined content, then mark the file as resolved with git add and complete the merge with git commit. A concrete scenario: you and a colleague both modified main. c in different branches, changing the same function header. During merge, Git flags conflicts; you open main. c, pick the correct logic or combine both improvements, stage, and commit. Remote repositories let you share commits with collaborators and keep safe backups. After creating a remote repository on a hosting platform, you connect it to your local project using git remote add origin remote_repository_URL. To upload your commits, use git push -u origin main where the -u flag sets the upstream branch so future pushes can use git push without specifying origin. To bring changes from the remote into your local branch use git pull origin main. Pull is a convenience that fetches changes and then merges them into your current branch. A concrete use case: when a teammate pushes a hotfix to main, you git pull to bring that fix into your local copy before you continue feature work. A common misconception is that push overwrites others automatically — push will be rejected if your local history is behind; in that case you must git pull and resolve differences before pushing. For safety, avoid force-pushing unless you understand history rewriting and its consequences for collaborators. Remote repositories: push and pull means use git remote add, git push, and git pull to share work and stay up to date; handle divergent history carefully.. A. gitignore file tells Git which files or patterns to ignore so they are not tracked. For C projects you typically ignore compiled object files, executables, and temporary build artifacts. Example entries are '*. o' to ignore object files and 'a. out' or your binary name to ignore compiled executables. Beyond build artifacts,. gitignore is critical for preventing accidental commits of sensitive configuration or A P I keys. If you accidentally stage a file with secrets, use git restore --staged to remove it from staging and git restore to revert your working copy to the last committed state. A key safety rule is: never commit secrets to a public repository. If a secret was committed previously, removing it from history is more complex and requires rewriting history and careful coordination with collaborators. Therefore, put. gitignore in place early, and verify with git status that sensitive files are not tracked. Here are the three compact concepts to anchor your practice. First, the three Git areas — working directory, staging area, and local repository — form the mental model you will use every day. Mastering this model helps you stage precisely and commit purposefully. Second, branching and merging are the primary tools for isolated feature development and safe integration. Create branches frequently, keep them focused, and resolve conflicts by testing and deliberate edits. Third, remote workflows and safety matter: use git remote, git push, and git pull to collaborate and back up work, and use. gitignore to prevent accidental commits of compiled files or secrets. These ideas together make your development reproducible, auditable, and collaborative.
